1 The data

L09_workshops.csv records one month of activity for the 320 artisan workshops that belong to a regional consortium. Every statement made below describes these 320 workshops exactly: nothing is inferred about workshops outside the file.

Column Meaning
workshop_id Identifier of the workshop
province_code Province of registration, coded 1 to 4
craft Craft practised: Ceramics, Leather, Woodwork, Textiles
qualification Level held by the head of the workshop: Apprentice, Craftsman, Master
years_active Completed years the workshop has been active
price_per_piece List price of a piece, averaged over the workshop’s catalogue, in euros
pieces_sold Pieces sold during the month
quality_score Consortium quality score for the month, from 1 to 5
monthly_revenue Total takings for the month, in euros: sales net of discounts, plus commissions, courses and repairs
exports Whether the workshop sold abroad during the month

Because of discounts on one side and non-sales income on the other, monthly_revenue is not the product of price_per_piece and pieces_sold.

Four exercises. Fill the chunks; the questions that close each one are there for you to check your own understanding, and are not handed in.

workshops <- read.csv("L09_workshops.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

str(workshops)

2 Exercise 1 — Measurement scales, position and shape

  1. Run summary() on the data frame and identify the column with missing values and how many there are.
  2. Compute mean(workshops$province_code). Then convert qualification into an ordered factor with its levels in the correct order and check it with table().
  3. Compute mean, median and the five-number summary of monthly_revenue, and the sample skewness 1n∑izi3\frac{1}{n}\sum_i z_i^3, where ziz_i is the standardized variable computed with mean() and sd().
  4. Recompute mean and median after removing the largest workshop, with workshops$monthly_revenue[-which.max(workshops$monthly_revenue)], and compare the two displacements.

revenue <- workshops$monthly_revenue
revenue_mean <- mean(revenue)
revenue_median <- median(revenue)
z <- (revenue - mean(revenue)) / sd(revenue)
revenue_skewness <- mean(z^3)

print(c(Mean_EUR = revenue_mean, Median_EUR = revenue_median,
        Sample_skewness = revenue_skewness))

# This expression removes exactly one observation; keep the full dataset intact.
revenue_without_largest <-
  workshops$monthly_revenue[-which.max(workshops$monthly_revenue)]
stopifnot(length(revenue_without_largest) == length(revenue) - 1)
mean_without_largest <- mean(revenue_without_largest)
median_without_largest <- median(revenue_without_largest)

print(data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean (EUR)", "Median (EUR)"),
  Full_data = c(revenue_mean, revenue_median),
  Largest_removed = c(mean_without_largest, median_without_largest),
  Change_removed_minus_full = c(mean_without_largest - revenue_mean,
                               median_without_largest - revenue_median)
))
##      Statistic Full_data Largest_removed Change_removed_minus_full

## 2 Median (EUR)  6879.860        6872.780                  -7.08000

(a) Classify province_code, qualification, years_active and monthly_revenue on the four measurement scales, and state for each the highest admissible measure of centre. Why did R return a number for the mean of province_code? (b) What does the sign of the skewness, together with the relative position of mean and median, say about the distribution of the revenue? (c) Which of the two summaries moved when the largest workshop was removed, and which property accounts for it?

3 Exercise 2 — Variability and concentration

  1. Compute the standard deviation and the IQR of monthly_revenue, and the coefficient of variation s/x‾s/\bar{x} of monthly_revenue, pieces_sold and price_per_piece.
  2. For k=1.5,2,3k = 1.5, 2, 3, compute the observed proportion of values within kk standard deviations of the mean and compare it with the Bienaymé–Chebyshev bound 1−1/k21 - 1/k^2.
  3. Draw the Lorenz curve of monthly_revenue and compute the Gini index as twice the area between the diagonal and the curve:
x <- sort(workshops$monthly_revenue)
p <- (0:length(x)) / length(x)          # cumulative share of workshops
q <- c(0, cumsum(x)) / sum(x)           # cumulative share of total revenue
plot(p, q, type = "l"); abline(0, 1, lty = 2)

area <- sum(diff(p) * (head(q, -1) + tail(q, -1)) / 2)
1 - 2 * area

Read off the share of the total taken by the poorer half and by the top decile.

  1. Draw the histogram of monthly_revenue with breaks = 10 and with breaks = 60. Assign each call to an object and report, for both, the number of classes actually drawn, length(h$counts), and their width, diff(h$breaks)[1].
revenue <- workshops$monthly_revenue
print(c(SD_EUR = sd(revenue), IQR_EUR = IQR(revenue)))
##   SD_EUR  IQR_EUR 
## 4327.060 5097.975
cv_variables <- c("monthly_revenue", "pieces_sold", "price_per_piece")
cv <- sapply(workshops[cv_variables], function(x) sd(x) / mean(x))
print(data.frame(Variable = names(cv), CV = unname(cv)))
##          Variable        CV
## 1 monthly_revenue 0.5473491
## 2     pieces_sold 0.3202583
## 3 price_per_piece 0.2260644
k <- c(1.5, 2, 3)
observed_proportion <- sapply(k, function(ki) {
  mean(abs(revenue - mean(revenue)) <= ki * sd(revenue))
})
chebyshev_bound <- 1 - 1 / k^2
print(data.frame(
  k = k,
  Observed_proportion = observed_proportion,
  Chebyshev_lower_bound = chebyshev_bound,
  Observed_minus_bound = observed_proportion - chebyshev_bound
))
##     k Observed_proportion Chebyshev_lower_bound Observed_minus_bound
## 1 1.5            0.893750             0.5555556            0.3381944
## 2 2.0            0.943750             0.7500000            0.1937500
## 3 3.0            0.990625             0.8888889            0.1017361
x <- sort(workshops$monthly_revenue)
p <- (0:length(x)) / length(x)
q <- c(0, cumsum(x)) / sum(x)
# A square plotting region keeps both cumulative-share axes between 0 and 1.
old_pty <- par("pty")
par(pty = "s")
plot(p, q, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#245E85", asp = 1,
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     main = "Lorenz curve of monthly revenue",
     xlab = "Cumulative share of workshops",
     ylab = "Cumulative share of total revenue")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topleft", c("Monthly revenue", "Equal-revenue diagonal"),
       col = c("#245E85", "grey50"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

par(pty = old_pty)

# Trapezoids give the area under the empirical Lorenz curve.
area <- sum(diff(p) * (head(q, -1) + tail(q, -1)) / 2)
gini <- 1 - 2 * area
print(c(Lorenz_area = area, Gini_index = gini))
## Lorenz_area  Gini_index 
##   0.3519760   0.2960479
# For 320 workshops, these groups contain exactly 160 and 32 observations.
bottom_n <- length(x) / 2
top_n <- length(x) / 10
bottom50_share <- sum(head(x, bottom_n)) / sum(x)
top10_share <- sum(tail(x, top_n)) / sum(x)
print(data.frame(
  Group = c("Bottom 50%", "Top 10%"),
  Workshops = c(bottom_n, top_n),
  Revenue_share = c(bottom50_share, top10_share),
  Revenue_percent = 100 * c(bottom50_share, top10_share)
))
##        Group Workshops Revenue_share Revenue_percent
## 1 Bottom 50%       160     0.2936911        29.36911
## 2    Top 10%        32     0.2195749        21.95749
h10 <- hist(revenue, breaks = 10, col = "#9DBDD2", border = "white",
            main = "Monthly revenue: breaks = 10",
            xlab = "Monthly revenue (EUR)", ylab = "Number of workshops")

h60 <- hist(revenue, breaks = 60, col = "#9DBDD2", border = "white",
            main = "Monthly revenue: breaks = 60",
            xlab = "Monthly revenue (EUR)", ylab = "Number of workshops")

print(data.frame(
  Requested_breaks = c(10, 60),
  Actual_bins = c(length(h10$counts), length(h60$counts)),
  Bin_width_EUR = c(diff(h10$breaks)[1], diff(h60$breaks)[1])
))
##   Requested_breaks Actual_bins Bin_width_EUR
## 1               10          13          2000
## 2               60          49           500

(a) Why can the standard deviations of monthly_revenue and pieces_sold not be compared directly, and what does the coefficient of variation change? (b) The observed proportions exceed the Chebyshev bounds by a wide margin. Is that a defect of the inequality, of the data, or of neither? (c) What does the Gini index measure that the standard deviation does not? Which of the two histograms would you use, and why is the choice not neutral?

4 Exercise 3 — Association between two categorical variables

  1. Build the contingency table of qualification by craft and the conditional distribution of qualification within each craft (prop.table(tab, margin = 2)).
  2. Compute the chi-square statistic with chisq.test() and Cramér’s V, V=χ2/(n⋅(min⁡(r,c)−1))V = \sqrt{\chi^2 / (n \cdot (\min(r,c) - 1))}.
  3. Measure the dependence in mean of price_per_piece on qualification through eta-squared, the ratio of the between-group deviance to the total deviance, and draw the box-plots of price_per_piece by qualification:
grand_mean  <- mean(workshops$price_per_piece)
group_means <- tapply(workshops$price_per_piece, workshops$qualification, mean)
group_n     <- table(workshops$qualification)

sum(group_n * (group_means - grand_mean)^2) /
  sum((workshops$price_per_piece - grand_mean)^2)
tab <- table(workshops$qualification, workshops$craft)
print(tab)
##             
##              Ceramics Leather Textiles Woodwork
##   Apprentice       13      43       48       31
##   Craftsman        21      32       20       31
##   Master           27      19        7       28
conditional <- prop.table(tab, margin = 2)
print(conditional)
##             
##                Ceramics    Leather   Textiles   Woodwork
##   Apprentice 0.21311475 0.45744681 0.64000000 0.34444444
##   Craftsman  0.34426230 0.34042553 0.26666667 0.34444444
##   Master     0.44262295 0.20212766 0.09333333 0.31111111
# The supplied setup hides warnings, so capture and report any test warning.
chi_warnings <- character(0)
chi <- withCallingHandlers(
  chisq.test(tab),
  warning = function(w) {
    chi_warnings <<- c(chi_warnings, conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
print(chi)
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test
## 
## data:  tab
## X-squared = 35.73, df = 6, p-value = 3.111e-06
n <- sum(tab)
r <- nrow(tab)
c <- ncol(tab)
cramers_v <- sqrt(unname(chi$statistic) / (n * (min(r, c) - 1)))
print(c(Cramers_V = cramers_v))
## Cramers_V 
##  0.236279
cat("Expected counts:\n")
## Expected counts:
print(chi$expected)
##             
##              Ceramics  Leather Textiles Woodwork
##   Apprentice 25.73438 39.65625 31.64062 37.96875
##   Craftsman  19.82500 30.55000 24.37500 29.25000
##   Master     15.44063 23.79375 18.98438 22.78125
print(c(Minimum_expected = min(chi$expected),
        Cells_below_5 = sum(chi$expected < 5),
        Cells_below_1 = sum(chi$expected < 1)))
## Minimum_expected    Cells_below_5    Cells_below_1 
##         15.44063          0.00000          0.00000
cat("All expected counts are at least 5:", all(chi$expected >= 5), "\n")
## All expected counts are at least 5: TRUE
cat("Chi-square warnings:",
    if (length(chi_warnings)) paste(chi_warnings, collapse = "; ") else "none",
    "\n")
## Chi-square warnings: none
cat("Each workshop has one record; independence between workshops cannot",
    "be established from the contingency table alone.\n")
## Each workshop has one record; independence between workshops cannot be established from the contingency table alone.
grand_mean <- mean(workshops$price_per_piece)
group_means <- tapply(workshops$price_per_piece, workshops$qualification, mean)
group_n <- table(workshops$qualification)
between_deviance <- sum(group_n * (group_means - grand_mean)^2)
total_deviance <- sum((workshops$price_per_piece - grand_mean)^2)
eta_squared <- between_deviance / total_deviance
print(c(Between_group_deviance = between_deviance,
        Total_deviance = total_deviance, Eta_squared = eta_squared))
## Between_group_deviance         Total_deviance            Eta_squared 
##           4.972662e+04           6.721680e+04           7.397945e-01
boxplot(price_per_piece ~ qualification, data = workshops,
        main = "Price per piece by qualification",
        xlab = "Qualification (ordered)", ylab = "Price per piece (EUR)",
        col = c("#C9DBE8", "#91B5CD", "#5689AE"))

(a) Why is a comparison of the raw counts not evidence of association, and which comparison is? What would independence in distribution look like in the table of conditional distributions? (b) Which of χ2\chi^2 and VV would be roughly unchanged if the consortium had ten times as many workshops with the same percentage profile, and why? (c) Interpret the value of eta-squared in one sentence.

5 Exercise 4 — Association between two quantitative variables

  1. Compute the Pearson and the Spearman correlation matrices for years_active, price_per_piece, pieces_sold, quality_score and monthly_revenue (use = "complete.obs"), and subtract the first from the second.
  2. Plot quality_score against pieces_sold and compute the Pearson correlation of the pair.
variables <- c("years_active", "price_per_piece", "pieces_sold",
               "quality_score", "monthly_revenue")
quantitative <- workshops[variables]
cat("Complete observations for both matrices:",
    sum(complete.cases(quantitative)), "of", nrow(workshops), "\n")
## Complete observations for both matrices: 309 of 320
pearson <- cor(quantitative, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs")
spearman <- cor(quantitative, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
correlation_difference <- spearman - pearson
cat("Pearson correlation matrix:\n")
## Pearson correlation matrix:
print(pearson, digits = 4)
##                 years_active price_per_piece pieces_sold quality_score
## years_active         1.00000         0.92493    -0.04413      -0.03094
## price_per_piece      0.92493         1.00000    -0.05259      -0.06752
## pieces_sold         -0.04413        -0.05259     1.00000      -0.12429
## quality_score       -0.03094        -0.06752    -0.12429       1.00000
## monthly_revenue      0.33184         0.39931     0.46052      -0.06826
##                 monthly_revenue
## years_active            0.33184
## price_per_piece         0.39931
## pieces_sold             0.46052
## quality_score          -0.06826
## monthly_revenue         1.00000
cat("Spearman correlation matrix:\n")
## Spearman correlation matrix:
print(spearman, digits = 4)
##                 years_active price_per_piece pieces_sold quality_score
## years_active         1.00000         0.96931    -0.04023      -0.07551
## price_per_piece      0.96931         1.00000    -0.06090      -0.08959
## pieces_sold         -0.04023        -0.06090     1.00000      -0.15784
## quality_score       -0.07551        -0.08959    -0.15784       1.00000
## monthly_revenue      0.38179         0.40107     0.45792      -0.06519
##                 monthly_revenue
## years_active            0.38179
## price_per_piece         0.40107
## pieces_sold             0.45792
## quality_score          -0.06519
## monthly_revenue         1.00000
cat("Difference: Spearman minus Pearson:\n")
## Difference: Spearman minus Pearson:
print(correlation_difference, digits = 4)
##                 years_active price_per_piece pieces_sold quality_score
## years_active        0.000000        0.044377    0.003906     -0.044570
## price_per_piece     0.044377        0.000000   -0.008310     -0.022073
## pieces_sold         0.003906       -0.008310    0.000000     -0.033551
## quality_score      -0.044570       -0.022073   -0.033551      0.000000
## monthly_revenue     0.049950        0.001762   -0.002593      0.003072
##                 monthly_revenue
## years_active           0.049950
## price_per_piece        0.001762
## pieces_sold           -0.002593
## quality_score          0.003072
## monthly_revenue        0.000000
# Remove incomplete pairs together so the two vectors remain aligned.
pair <- workshops[complete.cases(workshops[c("quality_score", "pieces_sold")]),
                  c("quality_score", "pieces_sold")]
pair_r <- cor(pair$pieces_sold, pair$quality_score, method = "pearson")
print(c(Complete_pairs = nrow(pair), Pearson_r = pair_r))
## Complete_pairs      Pearson_r 
##    309.0000000     -0.1242937
plot(pair$pieces_sold, pair$quality_score,
     pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#245E85", alpha.f = 0.6),
     main = sprintf("Quality score against pieces sold\nPearson r = %.4f; n = %d",
                    pair_r, nrow(pair)),
     xlab = "Pieces sold during the month",
     ylab = "Consortium quality score (1 to 5)")

(a) Which variable appears in the two largest Spearman–Pearson gaps, and what does a positive gap indicate about the form of the relationship? (b) The correlation between quality_score and pieces_sold is close to zero. Does it follow that the two variables are unrelated?
